html:
The first Arab siege of Constantinople was a series of attacks by the Umayyad Caliphate on the Byzantine capital, traditionally dated 674 to 678. Caliph Mu'awiya I, who had won the Muslim civil war in 661, hoped to end the Byzantine Empire with one blow.

Arab fleets set up a base at Cyzicus on the Sea of Marmara and blockaded the city each summer. The walls held, and the new Greek fire burned much of the Arab fleet. On the way home storms wrecked more ships, and Mu'awiya made peace with Emperor Constantine IV, agreeing to pay a yearly tribute.

Some modern historians think the story, told mainly by Theophanes the Confessor a century later, joins several smaller campaigns into one long siege. Either way, it was the first great check to the Arab conquests in the east. A larger attempt came in the siege of 717.
